# JSX Deep Dive ## Why This Matters JSX is the syntax that every React developer writes daily. Understanding exactly what JSX compiles to, how it relates to JavaScript, and its edge cases separates the "just enough to get by" developer from the engineer who can debug mysterious rendering issues and ace high‑stakes interviews. At FAANG companies, you will be asked to explain JSX internals, not just use it. ## Interview Frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Very High) – Expect JSX questions in phone screens, onsite coding, and even senior system design discussions. ## Learning Objectives - Understand JSX as syntactic sugar for `React.createElement` - Embed expressions, conditionals, and loops correctly - Recognize JSX‑specific attribute names (`className`, `htmlFor`, camelCase) - Explain how JSX prevents XSS attacks - Trace the compilation path from JSX to React element objects - Debug common JSX mistakes and know the under‑the‑hood transformation ## Deep Explanation JSX (JavaScript XML) lets us write HTML‑like syntax inside JavaScript files. It is not a string template or a separate language – it’s a syntax extension that transpiles to standard JavaScript function calls. ### Under the Hood: From JSX to React.createElement When you write: ```jsx const element =

Hello, world!

; ``` a compiler (Babel or TypeScript) transforms it into: ```js const element = React.createElement( 'h1', { className: 'greeting' }, 'Hello, world!' ); ``` `React.createElement` returns a plain JavaScript object – a **React element**: ```js { $$typeof: Symbol.for('react.element'), type: 'h1', key: null, ref: null, props: { className: 'greeting', children: 'Hello, world!' } } ``` This object describes what you want to see on the screen. React reads it to build its Virtual DOM tree. ### ASCII Diagram: The Transformation Pipeline ``` JSX Code │ ▼ Babel / TypeScript │ ▼ React.createElement() calls │ ▼ React Element Objects (Virtual DOM nodes) │ ▼ React Reconciler (Fiber) ``` ### Component Elements When you use a user‑defined component, the `type` becomes the function itself: ```jsx function Welcome(props) { return

Hello, {props.name}

; } const el = ; ``` Compiles to: ```js const el = React.createElement(Welcome, { name: 'Sara' }); ``` React will later call `Welcome(props)` during rendering. This is why component names **must** start with a capital letter – lower‑case tags become strings, upper‑case become variable references. ### Expressions in JSX Anything inside curly braces `{}` must be a valid JavaScript **expression** (something that produces a value). Statements like `if`/`for` are not allowed. ```jsx const name = 'React';

Hello, {name.toUpperCase()}

// Hello, REACT ``` You can even use immediately‑invoked function expressions (IIFE), though that’s usually a code smell. ### Conditionals Because `if` doesn’t work, we use ternary operators, logical `&&`, or conditionally returning JSX. **Good:** ```jsx {isLoggedIn ? : } {unreadMessages.length > 0 && } ``` **Bad (syntax error):** ```jsx {if (isLoggedIn) { }} // ❌ ``` When using `&&`, beware of falsy values like `0`. React renders `0` literally: ```jsx {items.length && } // if length is 0, it renders '0' instead of nothing! ``` Better: `{items.length > 0 && }` ### Loops with `.map()` ```jsx const todos = ['Learn JSX', 'Build apps'];
    {todos.map((todo, index) =>
  • {todo}
    • )}
``` Always provide a **key** prop to help React identify which items changed, were added, or removed. Keys should be stable, unique, and predictable (avoid array index if order changes). ### JSX Quirks and Attribute Naming | HTML | JSX | Reason | |-----------------|---------------|-------------------------------------| | `class` | `className` | `class` is a reserved word in JS | | `for` | `htmlFor` | `for` is a reserved word in JS | | `tabindex` | `tabIndex` | camelCase for DOM API consistency | | `onclick` | `onClick` | camelCase event handlers | | `style="color:red"` | `style={{ color: 'red' }}` | JavaScript object with camelCase properties | Self‑closing tags are mandatory: ``, `
`, ``. ### JSX Security: Automatic XSS Protection React DOM escapes any values embedded in JSX before rendering them. It converts characters like `<`, `>`, `&` to their HTML entities. ```jsx const userInput = ''; const element =
{userInput}
; // Renders as the literal text, not an image tag ``` This means you can safely render user‑generated content without creating XSS vulnerabilities, unless you use `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. ### Fragments Adjacent JSX elements must be wrapped in a single parent. Use `<>` (Fragment) to avoid adding extra DOM nodes: ```jsx <>
``` Fragments can have a `key` attribute only when using the explicit `` syntax. ## Production Example A real‑world profile card component: ```jsx function UserProfile({ user, isEditable }) { return (

{user.name}

{user.bio &&

{user.bio}

} {isEditable && }
); } ``` ## Best Practices - Wrap multi‑line JSX in parentheses for readability. - Keep JSX expressions simple; extract complex logic to variables or helper functions. - Use `null` when you want to render nothing. - Prefer `ternary` over complex `&&` chains. - Always add meaningful `alt` attributes and accessible labels. - Use fragments to avoid unnecessary wrapper divs. ## Common Mistakes - Forgetting to close self‑closing tags (`` is fine in HTML but JSX requires ``) - Using `class` instead of `className` - Embedding objects directly (they convert to `[object Object]`) - Not providing keys, or using unstable keys like array indices when order changes - Assuming `0` or empty string will be treated as `false` with `&&` - Writing inline arrow functions that cause extra re‑renders ## Interview Tips - Always start with “JSX is syntactic sugar for `React.createElement`.” - Walk through the compilation output: JSX → `React.createElement` → React element object. - Mention the security benefit (automatic escaping). - Be ready to explain key prop, fragments, and the difference between a React element and a component instance. ## Live Coding Exercise **Task:** Build a `UserList` component that receives an array of user names and a `filterText` prop. Render only names that include the filter text (case‑insensitive), each with a delete button. Use `key`, conditional rendering (empty state message), and avoid index as key if possible (assume names are unique). ## Mock Interview Question **"What is JSX and how does it relate to JavaScript?"** A strong answer: “JSX is a syntax extension that looks like HTML but transpiles to plain JavaScript. Each JSX tag becomes a `React.createElement` call that returns a lightweight object describing what should be rendered. It’s not a template engine – it’s fully integrated with JavaScript, enabling the full power of JS inside the markup through expressions.” ## Cheatsheet - JSX → `React.createElement(type, props, ...children)` - `className`, `htmlFor`, camelCase event handlers - `{}` for expressions, `ternary`/`&&` for conditionals - `.map()` + `key` for lists - Fragment: `<>` - All tags must be closed - JSX prevents XSS by escaping embedded values ## Mastery Checklist - [ ] Can explain what JSX compiles to - [ ] Write conditionals and loops without hesitation - [ ] Know all attribute naming differences - [ ] Choose correct key for each list item - [ ] Understand how JSX protects against XSS - [ ] Can refactor a class‑based old code to modern JSX patterns

# Answers ## 1. What is JSX, and what does it compile to? **Correct Answer:** JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that looks like HTML. It compiles to `React.createElement` function calls, which return plain JavaScript objects called React elements. These elements describe the UI structure. **Step‑by‑Step:** 1. Write JSX: `
Hello
` 2. Babel/TypeScript transpiles it to: `React.createElement('div', { className: 'box' }, 'Hello')` 3. `React.createElement` returns: ```json { $$typeof: Symbol.for('react.element'), type: 'div', key: null, ref: null, props: { className: 'box', children: 'Hello' } } ``` 4. React uses this element to update the DOM. **Interview Perspective:** A candidate who stops at “it’s HTML in JavaScript” shows shallow knowledge. You must explain the compilation step and the resulting object. **Common Mistakes:** - Believing JSX is a template language like Handlebars. - Thinking JSX is directly understood by the browser. ## 2. Why `className` instead of `class`? **Correct Answer:** `class` is a reserved keyword in JavaScript (for class declarations). To avoid syntax conflicts, JSX uses the DOM property name `className`. Similarly, `for` becomes `htmlFor`, and event handlers use camelCase (`onClick`, `onChange`). **Other differences:** - `tabindex` → `tabIndex` - `accesskey` → `accessKey` - `style` is an object, e.g., `style={{ color: 'red' }}` **Interview Perspective:** This demonstrates you understand both JavaScript and DOM API conventions. A follow‑up could be about how React attributes map to DOM properties, not HTML attributes. **Common Mistakes:** - Using `class` out of habit and then being confused by the console warning. - Forgetting to camelCase SVG attributes like `stroke-width` → `strokeWidth`. ## 3. Rendering `{true}` **Correct Answer:** React renders nothing (empty output). `true`, `false`, `null`, `undefined` are valid React children that produce no DOM. **Why:** React does not render these values; they are treated as “nothing”. This is intentional for conditional rendering patterns (`{condition && }`). **Common Mistake:** Expecting it to render the string "true". ## 4. The `key` Prop **Correct Answer:** `key` helps React identify which items have changed, been added, or removed in a list. It gives each element a stable identity, enabling efficient reconciliation and preventing unnecessary re‑renders or state mismatches. **When index is acceptable:** The list is static, items never change order or are added/removed, and items have no IDs. Still, using a unique ID is always safer. **When index is dangerous:** Re‑ordering, filtering, or inserting items can cause components to reuse state incorrectly (e.g., an input’s value stays in the same position after sorting). **Interview Perspective:** Explain reconciliation: without keys, React reuses elements based on index, which leads to bugs in controlled inputs or animations. You should mention the concept of "stable identity". **Common Mistakes:** - Forgetting the key entirely (React uses index and warns). - Using `Math.random()` – key changes every render, destroying performance and state. - Using an object as key (it becomes `[object Object]`). ## 5. Debug: `{user}` **Correct Answer:** The screen shows "Welcome, [object Object]". JSX expressions are converted to strings when placed directly. An object’s default string representation is `[object Object]`. **Fix:** Access the property you want: `{user.name}`. **Why:** JSX doesn’t automatically destructure or iterate objects. It simply calls `toString()` on the expression result. **Interview Perspective:** This catches developers who don’t test edge cases. The fix is simple; the lesson is to always check what you’re embedding. ## 6. XSS Prevention **Correct Answer:** React DOM automatically escapes any values interpolated into JSX. It converts characters like `<`, `>`, `&` into HTML entities during the render phase, making it impossible for a raw string to be executed as HTML unless you use `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. **Example:** ```jsx const dangerous = ''; const element =
{dangerous}
; // Renders as text: <img src=x onerror=alert(1)> ``` **Why other methods might fail:** Server‑side templates often require manual escaping. React’s default safety is a huge security win. **Common Mistakes:** - Using `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` without sanitization. - Assuming all JavaScript frameworks do this automatically (some don’t). ## 7. Rewrite with ternary **Correct Answer:** ```jsx return
{loggedIn ? : }
; ``` **Why:** Ternary is an expression, so it can be placed inside `{}`. The imperative if/else returns a value, but can’t appear directly inside JSX blocks. **Common Mistake:** Forgetting the enclosing `{}`: ```jsx // Wrong
loggedIn ? :
``` This would render the literal string. ## 8. Fragment and Key **Correct Answer:** A Fragment (`<>` or ``) groups multiple elements without adding extra DOM nodes. You can use a Fragment with a key only when using ``. **Use cases:** - Return multiple elements from a component without a wrapper div. - Avoid breaking CSS layout or adding unnecessary nesting. **Why not `<>` with key:** The shorthand syntax does not accept props. **Interview Perspective:** Shows you care about DOM cleanliness and know the advanced syntax. ## 9. Filter and render list starting with 'A' **Correct Answer:** ```jsx function AList({ items }) { const filtered = items.filter(item => item.toLowerCase().startsWith('a')); return (
    {filtered.map(item =>
  • {item}
    • )}
); } ``` **Why:** Extract filtering logic outside JSX for readability. Use `key={item}` only if items are unique strings; otherwise, add a unique identifier. ## 10. Is JSX mandatory? **Correct Answer:** No, JSX is not mandatory. React can be used with plain `React.createElement` directly. However, JSX provides a more readable, HTML‑like syntax and is the standard in the community. **Without JSX example:** ```js const element = React.createElement('div', { className: 'app' }, React.createElement('h1', null, 'Hello World') ); ``` **When would you use it?** Very rare: maybe in environments without a build step, or embedded React usage where you want zero compilation overhead. But it’s impractical for large UIs. **Interview Perspective:** This question tests if you understand that JSX is syntactic sugar. A senior engineer might discuss tradeoffs of build steps. ## 11. Live Coding Solution (Comment component) ```jsx function timeAgo(date) { const now = new Date(); const diff = Math.floor((now - date) / 1000); if (diff < 60) return 'just now'; const mins = Math.floor(diff / 60); if (mins < 60) return `${mins} min ago`; const hours = Math.floor(mins / 60); if (hours < 24) return `${hours} hours ago`; return `${Math.floor(hours / 24)} days ago`; } function Comment({ author, text, timestamp, isEdited }) { const initial = author.charAt(0).toUpperCase(); return (
{initial}
{author} {timeAgo(timestamp)} {isEdited && ( Edited )}

{text}

); } ``` **Key Points:** - Condition `{isEdited && ...}` renders the badge only when true. - Inline styles use camelCase properties and JS object syntax. - Helper function `timeAgo` kept outside component to avoid re‑creation. - The component is pure JSX inside a single return statement. **Senior Perspective:** Consider extracting the avatar circle into its own `Avatar` component for reusability. Also, discuss how `timeAgo` could be memoized if timestamps rarely change.

lessons.lessonMarkdown:
# Components and Composition ## Why This Matters Components are the atomic unit of React applications. Understanding how to properly design, compose, and reuse components is the foundation of every successful React codebase. At FAANG interviews, you will be asked to build features on the fly – your ability to decompose a UI into a hierarchy of components and choose the right composition pattern is what separates a junior from a senior candidate. ## Interview Frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Extremely High) – Component design appears in every React interview: from a simple TODO app to a full‑scale system design. ## Learning Objectives - Distinguish between elements, components, and instances - Build functional components that accept props and render JSX - Compose components together via nesting and the `children` prop - Use composition over inheritance to solve UI problems - Understand prop destructuring, default props, and spread operators - Avoid prop drilling by lifting state or using composition ## Deep Explanation ### What Exactly Is a Component? A React component is a JavaScript function (functional component) or class (legacy) that returns React elements describing what should appear on the screen. Think of it as a pure function: props go in, React elements come out. ```jsx function Greeting(props) { return

Hello, {props.name}!

; } ``` React calls this function with an object of props during rendering. It can be called multiple times – each call creates a new "instance" (a new subtree of elements). ### Component vs Element vs Instance - **Component:** The function definition (blueprint) - **Element:** The object returned by `React.createElement` (a description of what to render) - **Instance:** The concrete representation of a component in the tree (managed internally by the reconciler). With hooks, instances are often a set of state and effects. ### Props: One‑Way Data Flow Props (short for properties) are read‑only inputs. A component must never modify its own props. This enforces a unidirectional data flow, making the application predictable. ```jsx function UserInfo({ name, role }) { // destructuring return

{name} – {role}

; } ``` Pass any JavaScript value: strings, numbers, objects, functions, even other React elements. ### Composition Model React’s composition model is its secret weapon. Instead of creating deep inheritance trees like in classical OOP, you build small, reusable components and combine them like Lego blocks. **Using `children`:** ```jsx function Card({ children }) { return
{children}
; }

Title

Content

 ``` `children` is a special prop containing whatever is between the opening and closing tag. This pattern lets you create layouts, modals, and generic wrappers without knowing the inner content ahead of time. **Multiple slots via props:** ```jsx function SplitPane({ left, right }) { return (
{left}
{right}
); } } right={} /> ``` Here we pass elements as props – a more explicit form of composition. ### Specialization Through Composition Instead of inheritance (like `BaseButton` extending `Button`), React encourages you to build generic components and configure them via props. ```jsx function Button({ variant, children, ...rest }) { const className = `btn ${variant === 'primary' ? 'btn-primary' : 'btn-secondary'}`; return ; } ``` ### Props Defaults and Spread You can set default values for props using default parameters: ```jsx function Alert({ type = 'info', message }) { return
{message}
; } ``` Spread attributes (`...rest`) allows passing extra props to underlying DOM elements, reducing boilerplate. ### ASCII Diagram: Component Hierarchy ``` App │ ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ Header │ └─────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ Main │ │ ┌────┐ │ │ │List│ │ │ └────┘ │ └─────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ Footer │ └─────────┘ ``` Each box is a component. Data flows down via props; events bubble up via callbacks. ## Under the Hood When React encounters `` in JSX, it calls `Card(props)` during rendering. The returned elements are then diffed with the previous tree. The function component’s identity is used to manage state and effects across renders via hooks. ## Production Example: A Composable Modal ```jsx function Modal({ open, onClose, title, footer, children }) { if (!open) return null; return (
e.stopPropagation()}>

{title}

{children}
{footer &&
{footer}
}
); } // Usage Confirm}>

Are you sure? This action cannot be undone.

 ``` This component is reusable for any dialog, fully controlled, and composed with slots. ## Best Practices - Prefer functional components with hooks. - Keep components small and focused on a single responsibility. - Use explicit prop names; avoid spreading entire objects unless necessary. - Use composition before adding yet another prop; let consumers compose layouts. - Destructure props in function signature for readability. - Always provide a meaningful default for optional props. - Avoid rendering `undefined` directly; use `null` for intentional emptiness. ## Common Mistakes - Mutating props directly (`props.name = 'new'`) – props are read‑only. - Using too many props when a composition slot would be cleaner. - Nesting components inside each other (creating new functions on every render, breaking memoization). - Forgetting that `children` is a prop like any other; you can pass React elements, strings, or even functions. - Passing all props via spread to a DOM element and accidentally applying non‑standard attributes (like `fetchStatus`). - Ignoring accessibility: a composed layout must still manage focus, roles, and labels. ## Interview Tips - Always mention “composition over inheritance” when discussing component design. - Demonstrate how to refactor a deep prop chain using composition (slots) instead of just drilling. - Be ready to build a composable list, modal, or form wrapper from scratch during a live coding round. - Explain that components are functions, and you can use all JS techniques (higher‑order functions, closures) to create reusable behaviors. ## Live Coding Exercise **Task:** Build a `Tabs` component that accepts an array of `{ label, content }` objects and renders a tab bar. Only the content of the active tab should be rendered. Style it inline (or using simple classes). Extend it to support composition: allow users to use `` with child `` components instead of only an array prop. ## Mock Interview Question **"How would you design a reusable `List` component that can render a grid of items, a simple vertical list, or a carousel?"** A strong answer: “I’d use composition. The `List` component would accept a `renderItem` prop (or `children` as a function) to delegate rendering of each item to the parent. The layout variant could be controlled via a `variant` prop or by providing completely different wrapper components. For a carousel, I’d build a separate `Carousel` that uses `List` internally. This keeps responsibilities separated and the API flexible.” ## Cheatsheet - Component = function(props) → React element - `children` prop for nesting, explicit slots for complex layouts - Composition > inheritance - Props are read‑only; callbacks propagate changes up - Destructure for clarity: `function Comp({ title, children })` - Default values: `function Comp({ size = 'medium' })` - Use spread cautiously: `

# Props and PropTypes ## Why This Matters Props are the artery of React's one‑way data flow – every piece of data a component receives comes through props. Understanding how to define, validate, and use props correctly is not just about writing clean code; it’s about preventing bugs at scale. In interviews, you'll be asked to explain prop drilling, default behaviours, and why type‑checking is crucial. PropTypes, though being phased out in favour of TypeScript, still appear in legacy codebases and interview questions about runtime validation. ## Interview Frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐ (High) – Expect props‑related questions in phone screens, coding exercises, and discussions about component APIs. ## Learning Objectives - Pass data from parent to child via props - Destructure and use default props - Validate props with PropTypes (both functional and legacy patterns) - Explain the difference between props and state - Recognise common anti‑patterns (mutating props, missing defaults) - Understand why TypeScript often replaces PropTypes today ## Deep Explanation Props (short for "properties") are the input arguments to a React component. They are read‑only and are passed from the parent down to the child. A component must never modify its own props – that’s the rule for keeping the data flow predictable. ### Passing Props ```jsx function Greeting(props) { return

Hello, {props.name}

; } ``` Inside `Greeting`, `props` is an object: `{ name: 'Alice' }`. You can pass any valid JavaScript value: strings, numbers, booleans, objects, arrays, functions, and even React elements. ### Destructuring Props For readability, destructure props directly in the function signature: ```jsx function Greeting({ name, age }) { return

{name} is {age} years old

; } ``` ### Default Props If a prop might be omitted, provide a default using JavaScript default parameters: ```jsx function Button({ label = 'Click', onClick }) { return ; }

# Event Handling ## Why This Matters Handling user interactions (clicks, keystrokes, form submissions) is the bread and butter of React apps. In interviews you’ll be asked to handle events correctly, avoid common pitfalls, and explain the magic behind React’s Synthetic Event system. Solid event handling knowledge separates candidates who just get it working from those who write efficient, accessible, and bug‑free interactions. ## Interview Frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐ (High) – Expect event handling questions in any live coding challenge, especially around form submissions, list interactions, and custom hooks like `useClickOutside`. ## Learning Objectives - Handle events with JSX camelCase attributes (`onClick`, `onSubmit`) - Differentiate between React Synthetic Events and native DOM events - Pass extra arguments to event handlers using closures or bind - Prevent default browser behaviour and stop event propagation correctly - Understand event delegation and React’s unified event system - Use keyboard events for accessibility - Create custom event hooks (e.g., click outside, key press) ## Deep Explanation ### Basic Event Handling In JSX, event handlers are passed as props using camelCase names – they receive the event object as the first argument. ```jsx ``` The handler function can be defined inline or referenced by name: ```jsx // Reference (preferred for performance and readability) const handleClick = () => alert('Clicked!'); return ; // Inline arrow (fine for simple logic, but creates new function each render) ``` ### SyntheticEvent React wraps the browser’s native event in a `SyntheticEvent` object. This object has the same interface as a native event (stopPropagation, preventDefault, target, etc.) but works identically across browsers. ```jsx function handleSubmit(event) { event.preventDefault(); // stop page reload console.log(event.target); // DOM element } ``` **Important:** SyntheticEvent is pooled in legacy React (≤16). React 17+ removed event pooling, so you can access `event` properties asynchronously without calling `event.persist()`. However, to avoid stale references you should still capture values early if needed. ### Passing Arguments to Handlers When you need to send extra data, wrap the handler in an arrow function or use `.bind()`. ```jsx // Arrow function (creates new function per render) // .bind() (also creates new function, less common) ``` Performance note: Inline arrow functions are fine for most components. Only worry when passing them to heavily memoized child components (then use `useCallback`). ### Preventing Default and Stopping Propagation - `event.preventDefault()`: cancels the default browser action (e.g., form submission, link navigation). - `event.stopPropagation()`: stops the event from bubbling up to ancestor elements. React attaches all events at the root of the document, but `stopPropagation()` still works because React’s event system simulates bubbling. However, native events will still propagate. Mixing React and native events requires caution. ### Keyboard and Accessibility Always provide keyboard equivalents for mouse events. For example, a button with `onClick` automatically responds to Enter and Space. For custom elements (like a `
` acting as a button) you must add `role="button"`, `tabIndex={0}`, and `onKeyDown` to handle Space/Enter. ```jsx

# Conditional Rendering ## Why This Matters React apps are dynamic: they show/hide components, switch between loading states, and render different UIs based on data. Conditional rendering is the core technique to achieve this. In interviews, you’ll frequently be asked to implement features like "if the user is logged in, show the dashboard; otherwise, show the login". Knowing the patterns, pitfalls (especially with `&&` and falsy values), and performance implications will make you stand out. ## Interview Frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐ (High) – Appears in virtually every live coding task and many debugging questions. ## Learning Objectives - Render different JSX based on conditions using ternary, `&&`, and `if` statements - Handle loading, error, and empty states gracefully - Prevent common bugs caused by falsy values (0, empty string) - Choose the right pattern for readability and performance - Combine conditional rendering with component composition - Use conditional rendering with fragments and lists ## Deep Explanation React gives you multiple ways to conditionally render elements. Since JSX is just syntactic sugar for JavaScript, we can use any JavaScript expression that returns a React element (or `null`/`undefined`/`false` for nothing). ### 1. Ternary Operator Use for mutually exclusive renders (one thing or another): ```jsx return (
{isLoggedIn ? : }
); ``` Ternaries can be nested but that quickly harms readability. Extract complex logic to variables or helper functions. ### 2. Logical AND (&&) Render something only if the condition is truthy: ```jsx {unreadMessages.length > 0 && } ``` **Pitfall:** Be careful with numbers. If the left side evaluates to `0` or `NaN`, React will render that number literally. ```jsx {items.length && } // If items.length === 0, renders the string '0' – not nothing! ``` Fix it by ensuring a boolean: ```jsx {items.length > 0 && } // or {!!items.length && } ``` ### 3. If/Else Outside JSX For more complex logic, use good old `if`/`else` before the `return`: ```jsx function Profile({ user }) { if (!user) { return ; } return ; } ``` This approach returns early and keeps the main render simple. ### 4. Using Variables Store a React element in a variable conditionally: ```jsx let button; if (isEditing) { button = ; } else if (hasUnsavedChanges) { button = ; } else { button = ; } return
{button}
; ``` ### 5. Immediately Invoked Function Expressions (IIFE) Though rarely recommended, you can use an IIFE to run `if` inside JSX: ```jsx {(() => { if (status === 'loading') return ; if (status === 'error') return ; return ; })()} ``` Better: extract this logic into a helper function or component. ### Rendering Nothing Return `null`, `undefined`, or `false` to render nothing. `null` is the most explicit. ```jsx function WarningBanner({ warn }) { if (!warn) return null; return
Warning!
; } ``` ### Combining with Fragments When conditionally rendering multiple elements, wrap them in a Fragment: ```jsx {showDetails && ( <> )} ``` ### ASCII Diagram: Conditional Flow ``` Component receives props/state │ ▼ Check condition (if/ternary) / \ true false │ │ ▼ ▼ Element A Element B (or null) ``` ## Under the Hood Conditional rendering does not introduce any special React mechanism; it’s plain JavaScript controlling what the component function returns. React simply renders whatever the function returns. When a condition toggles, the returned elements differ, so the reconciler unmounts the old subtree and mounts the new one (or updates if the same component type). This is also why you must be careful with state: a component that conditionally disappears loses its state unless preserved (e.g., using the same key or keeping it mounted but hidden). ## Production Example: Async Status Handler ```jsx function AsyncContent({ status, data, error }) { if (status === 'loading') { return ; } if (status === 'error') { return ; } if (!data || data.length === 0) { return ; } return ; } ``` Each status (loading, error, empty, success) is handled clearly. No nested ternaries, easy to test and maintain. ## Best Practices - Prefer early returns for conditions that block rendering (e.g., no user, redirect). - Use ternary for simple if/else; use `if`/`else` before return for complex branching. - Ensure the left side of `&&` is a boolean to avoid rendering `0` or `''`. - Extract conditional logic into a variable or helper when it becomes hard to read. - For conditional attributes, use the same patterns: ```jsx

# Lists and Keys ## Why This Matters Rendering collections of data is one of the most common tasks in React. Whether it’s a list of notifications, a product catalog, or chat messages, you will use `.map()` and the `key` prop daily. Misusing keys is the #1 source of subtle state and performance bugs. In FAANG interviews, you’ll be grilled on what keys do, why they matter, and when array indices are acceptable (spoiler: almost never). ## Interview Frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Extremely High) – Expect at least one question about keys in every React interview. It often comes as a debugging scenario: “Why does my list keep mixing up state after sorting?” ## Learning Objectives - Render dynamic lists using `Array.prototype.map()` - Understand the role of the `key` prop in React’s reconciliation - Choose stable, unique, predictable keys for list items - Recognize bugs caused by missing or unstable keys - Know when using array index as a key is safe (and when it’s catastrophic) - Use keys correctly with fragments and nested lists - Optimize rendering with proper key assignment ## Deep Explanation ### Rendering Arrays of Data To render a list in React, you map over your data array and return JSX for each item. ```jsx const fruits = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Cherry']; function FruitList() { return (
    {fruits.map((fruit, index) => (
  • {fruit}
    • ))}
); } ``` Each child in the list must have a unique `key` prop. React uses keys to identify which items changed, were added, or removed. ### What Are Keys? A `key` is a special string attribute that gives each element a stable identity across renders. Keys help React’s reconciler determine whether an element is the same as before or a completely new one. **Important:** Keys are not passed to the component as props. They are internal to React. ### Why React Needs Keys When re‑rendering a list, React compares the new Virtual DOM tree with the previous one. Without keys, it can only match elements by their position in the array. This leads to issues: - **State corruption:** A component’s state might “stick” to the wrong item after reordering. - **Unnecessary re‑mounting:** Elements that should be updated get destroyed and recreated. - **Performance degradation:** React performs more work than necessary. With stable keys, React can correctly identify the same element even if its position changes, preserving state and minimizing DOM mutations. ### Rules for Choosing Keys - Keys must be **unique** among siblings (not globally). - Keys must be **stable** across renders (no random values or timestamps). - Keys should be **predictable** – derived from the data itself. **Best:** Use a unique identifier from your data (e.g., `user.id`). ```jsx {users.map(user => )} ``` **Good:** If no ID exists, combine several fields that together form a unique value (e.g., `email` + `name`). As a last resort, you might generate IDs when data arrives and use them. Avoid using array index unless the list is static, never reordered, and items have no state. ### The Index as Key Anti‑Pattern Using the array index (`key={index}`) is tempting but dangerous. If the list order changes, items are added/removed, or the list is filtered, the index of each item changes. React then mistakenly treats old items as new ones and vice versa. **Example of state corruption with index as key:** ```jsx function ToDoList() { const [todos, setTodos] = useState([ { id: 1, text: 'Learn React' }, { id: 2, text: 'Build projects' } ]); const addTodo = () => { setTodos([{ id: Date.now(), text: 'New Todo' }, ...todos]); // adds to front }; return (
    {todos.map((todo, index) => ( ))}
); } function TodoItem({ text }) { const [done, setDone] = useState(false); return (
  • setDone(!done)} /> {text}
    • ); } ``` After adding a new todo to the top, the previous first item (index 0) becomes index 1, but React sees the key `0` unchanged and keeps the old `done` state for that index. The checkbox state now belongs to the wrong text. Using `key={todo.id}` fixes this. ### Rendering Fragments in Lists When returning multiple elements from `.map()`, you can use a Fragment. The short syntax `<>` doesn’t accept a `key`, so you must use ``. ```jsx {items.map(item => (
    {item.term}
    {item.description}
     ))} ``` ### Nested Lists and Keys Each level of mapping needs its own keys, but they only need to be unique among direct siblings. A parent list and a nested list can reuse the same key value; there’s no conflict. ```jsx {categories.map(cat => (

    {cat.name}

      {cat.items.map(item => (
    • {item.name}
      • ))}
    ))} ``` ### Keys in JSX Map Shorthand When using `.map()` directly in JSX, the `key` must be on the outermost element being returned. ```jsx // ✅ Correct
      {items.map(item =>
    • {item.name}
      • )}
    // ❌ Wrong — key is not on the outermost returned element (if ListItem returns a
  • )
      {items.map(item => )}
    ``` In the second case, `key` is on the `` component, not the `
  • ` inside it. This is actually fine because `ListItem` itself is the component React tracks. React sees the `ListItem` element and its key. The component internally renders an `
  • ` without a key, which is fine because it’s a single root. ### Under the Hood: Reconciliation with Keys During reconciliation, React iterates over the children arrays of both the old and new fiber trees. It tries to match children based on keys first. If a child has moved, React knows it’s the same one and just moves the DOM node rather than recreating it. Without keys, React falls back to index-based matching, which is fragile. **ASCII Diagram: Reconciliation with Keys** ``` Old children: New children: key: "A" key: "B" key: "B" key: "A" A B B A With keys: React sees B moved to top → move DOM node, keep state. Without keys: React sees index 0 changed from A to B → unmount A, mount B (loss of state). ``` ## Production Example: Sortable Table ```jsx function DataTable({ rows, sortKey, onSort }) { return ( {columns.map(col => ( ))} {rows.map(row => ( ))}
    onSort(col.id)}> {col.label}
    {row.name} {row.email}
    ); } ``` Even when sorting changes the order of `rows`, the keys (`row.id`) stay consistent, so React preserves any DOM state (like focused input fields) and only reorders existing nodes. ## Best Practices - Always provide a key when rendering lists. - Use a unique, stable identifier from your data (like a database ID). - Avoid using array index if the list can change (add, remove, reorder). - Generate IDs at data creation time if no natural key exists (e.g., `crypto.randomUUID()`), but don’t generate keys inside render. - Use `React.Fragment` with a key when mapping to multiple elements. - Remember: keys help React identify items; they do not render in the DOM. - For static lists that never change, index may be acceptable – but even then, code often evolves. ## Common Mistakes - Forgetting to add a `key` entirely (React warns in console). - Using `Math.random()` or `Date.now()` in render – key changes every render, causing unmount/remount and losing state. - Using index as key in dynamic lists and then wondering why input states are mixed up. - Placing `key` on a child element inside the component instead of on the component itself when mapping. - Duplicate keys among siblings – causes unpredictable rendering. - Confusing key’s uniqueness scope: it’s only among siblings, not the whole app. ## Accessibility Considerations When rendering lists that update dynamically, consider using `aria-live="polite"` on the container if you want screen readers to announce additions/removals. Proper keys also ensure that focus is preserved on the correct item after reordering (though manual focus management may still be needed). ## Interview Tips - When asked to render a list, immediately add a `key` before writing any content. - Explain the reconciliation process: “React uses keys to match children across renders, preventing unnecessary unmounts and state loss.” - Use the checkbox list example to demonstrate index‑as‑key bugs. - Mention that keys are not passed as props; if you need the value, pass it separately. - Be ready to discuss the trade‑off between using IDs and generating UUIDs. ## Live Coding Exercise **Task:** Build a `ShoppingList` component that displays items with name and quantity. Each item has an `id`, `name`, and `quantity`. Add an input field to edit the quantity inline. Ensure that editing one item does not affect others when the list re‑renders (e.g., after adding a new item at the top). Use proper keys. ## Mock Interview Question **"Explain the importance of keys in React lists. What happens if you don’t provide them, and when is using the array index acceptable?"** Strong answer: “Keys give React a way to identify each element in a list between renders. Without keys, React falls back to comparing by index, which can lead to state corruption (like input values or component state mixing up) and poor performance because React unmounts and remounts components that only changed position. Using array index is only safe when the list is static – never reordered, filtered, or added/removed. In all other cases, use a unique, stable identifier from the data. I’ve seen bugs where a checkbox state stayed on the wrong item after sorting because index was used as key.” ## Cheatsheet - `{data.map(item => )}` - Keys must be unique among siblings, stable, predictable - No keys → index matching → state bugs - Index as key: OK only for static lists - `` for fragments in lists - Don’t generate keys with `Math.random()` inside render - Key is not passed as a prop ## Mastery Checklist - [ ] Can render a list with `.map()` and unique keys - [ ] Explain why keys are needed for reconciliation - [ ] Identify and fix index‑as‑key bugs - [ ] Use Fragment with key when necessary - [ ] Know when to generate IDs vs using index - [ ] Understand that keys don’t appear in the DOM or props
